extracted.intended_audience: ministers, policymakers, and informed readers considering British colonial policy (18th-century context)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidelines and evaluative principles for administering and legislating colonial trade and governance, as argued in an 18th-century political essay. Emphasizes prudence in regulation, attention to commercial effects, legal propriety, and evidence-based parliamentary decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation complexity tied to occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations for the colony trade ought not to be more nor fewer, nor more nor less complex, than the occasion requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade with colonies is largely a 'system of art and restriction' and therefore cannot always be 'few and simple.' Regulations should match practical needs rather than ideological simplicity; excess regulation can destroy commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive multiplicity of regulatory instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: He had so multiplied bonds, certificates, affidavits, warrants, sufferances, and cockets; had supported them with such severe penalties... that commerce must speedily have expired under them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplying paperwork, bonds, and severe penalties is an anti-pattern: it overburdens commerce, forces later repeal, and openly confesses prior legislative error (e.g., the 5 Geo. III preamble). Prudence recommends removing unnecessary procedural burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: All significant measures require consideration of commercial consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Four million of debt due to our merchants, the total cessation of a trade annually worth four million more... all these were very weighty accumulated considerations... before that sword was drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before resorting to force or sweeping punitive measures, weigh economic costs (debt, trade stoppage, revenue loss, effects on public credit and manufacture). Even a militarily feasible coercion can be disastrous economically and politically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give due weight to merchants' testimony and the trading interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The universal alarm of the whole trading body of England, will never be laughed at by them as an ill-grounded or a pretended panic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merchants' evidence about debts, suspension of trade, and loss of credit is material to parliamentary decision-making about colonial measures; dismissing such testimony risks grave practical error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid injudicious, precipitate, or illegal measures to suppress dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: The measures taken to suppress that spirit were as violent and licentious as the spirit itself; injudicious, precipitate, and some of them illegal. Instead of allaying, they tended infinitely to inflame the distemper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repressive actions that violate law or constitutional norms tend to exacerbate unrest. Policy must favor temperate, lawful remedies over harsh punishments that inflame popular feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect legal and constitutional proprieties in executive conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the worst of these was, the wanton and indiscriminate seizure of papers, even in cases where the safety of the state was not pretended in justification of so harsh a proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abuses of office (e.g., indiscriminate seizures) are repugnant to law and constitutional spirit and produce public jealousy; officials should take steps to clarify law and avoid extra-legal practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full transparency and disclosure to legislative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Every paper of office was laid upon the table of the two Houses; every denomination of men... attended at the bar. Such evidence never was laid before Parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive disclosure of official papers and evidence to Parliament leads to better-informed decisions; concealment of remonstrances or facts misleads legislative judgment and produces imprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assert principle but act on expediency when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: They resolved, as a preliminary to that repeal, to assert in the fullest and least equivocal terms the unlimited legislative right of this country over its colonies; and, having done this, to propose the repeal, on principles... of expediency, of equity, of lenity, and of the true interests present and future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain declaratory legal principles where politically important, but frame immediate policy (e.g., repeals or concessions) on grounds of expediency, equity, and long-term interest to preserve authority while avoiding destructive conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Govern in a manner consonant with colonists' temper and spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: People must be governed in a manner agreeable to their temper and disposition; and men of free character and spirit must be ruled with, at least, some condescension to this spirit and this character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy toward settler populations descended from free traditions should incorporate concessions and modes of governance that respect their character; purely coercive, restraint-heavy governance is neither wise nor practicable long-term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where monopoly or restraint exists, consider compensatory indulgences
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought rather to infer from our having laid the colonies under many restraints, that it is reasonable to compensate them by every indulgence that can by any means be reconciled to our interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an imperial power enforces commercial monopolies and restraints, it should offset burdens with reasonable indulgences to secure loyalty and practical subordination without inciting resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base parliamentary decisions on real evidence rather than partisan rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: If an emulation arose among the ministers and members of Parliament... it was not on the confident assertions, the airy speculations, or the vain promises of ministers, that it arose. It was the sense of Parliament on the evidence before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good policy outcomes follow from presenting factual testimony and broad, corroborated evidence to legislative bodies rather than from appeals to factional rhetoric or speculation.
